subject: HEALTH
overview: Semester 1 is driver education built on the current California Driver Handbook: read the assigned section, practice with diagrams, toy cars and in-car (parked) drills, then quiz; always defer to the latest handbook and DMV site if a rule has changed. Semester 2 covers first aid/CPR/AED (hands-on practice on a manikin or pillow, ideally followed by an official Red Cross or AHA certification) and Health II topics — mental health, suicide prevention, substances, nutrition, consumer and environmental health, relationships and sexual health. Preview sensitive weeks (24–29, 33–34) and use them to talk about your family's values while keeping the facts medically accurate.

weeks.prep: Download the current California Driver Handbook (dmv.ca.gov) and open the DMV 'Driver's Licenses' and 'Teen Drivers' pages. Read the licensing section yourself first, since rules are occasionally updated — the handbook is the authority if anything here differs. Print a blank driving log template.
misconceptions: Students think the provisional license is a full license. For the first 12 months, provisional drivers may not drive 11 p.m.–5 a.m. or carry passengers under 20 unless accompanied by a licensed parent/guardian, a licensed driver 25 or older, or a certified driving instructor (limited exceptions apply).
Students think the 50 practice hours can be any time of day. At least 10 of the 50 supervised hours must be at night.
Students think finishing driver education alone earns a permit. They must also apply, pass the vision and knowledge tests, and have a parent/guardian sign.

days.guide: Share a teen crash statistic from NHTSA or the CDC (drivers aged 16–19 have the highest crash rate per mile driven of any age group). Discuss how graduated licensing works in stages. The student writes a paragraph on why California uses GDL and three questions to answer this semester.

questions.q: Why do teens have higher crash rates?
questions.a: Inexperience (poor hazard recognition), higher risk-taking, distraction, and peer passengers; GDL limits the riskiest situations while experience builds.

questions.q: Name the stages of California's graduated licensing.
questions.a: Instruction permit → provisional license (with restrictions) → full license at 18.

days.guide: The student reads the handbook licensing section and lists every permit requirement in order: age 15½, driver education, application (online DL 44 form), identity, documents, fee, thumbprint and photo, vision test, knowledge test, parent signature.

questions.q: What tests must be passed to get a permit?
questions.a: A vision test and a written/online knowledge test on traffic laws and signs.

questions.q: Who must sign the application for a minor?
questions.a: A parent or legal guardian (both if there is joint custody).

days.guide: The student creates a one-page chart of provisional license restrictions and exceptions. Quiz orally from the chart.

questions.q: You are 16 with a provisional license for 4 months. Can you drive your 17-year-old friend to the movies alone?
questions.a: No — for the first 12 months you cannot carry passengers under 20 without a licensed parent/guardian, a licensed driver 25 or older, or an instructor.

questions.q: Can you drive home from work at 11:30 p.m.?
questions.a: Only with a signed note from your employer (a work exception), or with an accompanying licensed adult 25+.

days.guide: Together, build a practice log template with columns for date, time, hours, night (Y/N), conditions and skills practiced, and plan when the 50 hours (10 at night) and 6 hours of professional training will happen.

questions.q: How many supervised hours are required, and how many at night?
questions.a: 50 hours, including at least 10 at night.

questions.q: How long must you hold your permit before taking the drive test?
questions.a: At least 6 months.

days.guide: Give the 15-question quiz. Grade together; the student finds the handbook page for each missed item.

questions.q: When do the provisional restrictions on passengers and night driving end?
questions.a: After 12 months of holding the provisional license.

weeks.assessment_key: Licensing quiz key (15 items): 1) Minimum age for a permit — 15½. 2) Driver education required before the permit — yes, completed (or enrolled in) a state-approved course. 3) Parent/guardian signature required — yes. 4) Tests at the permit appointment — vision and knowledge test. 5) Minimum time holding a permit before the drive test — 6 months. 6) Supervised practice — 50 hours, 10 at night. 7) Professional behind-the-wheel training — 6 hours (required for applicants under 17½). 8) Minimum age for a provisional license — 16. 9) Who must accompany a permit driver — a California-licensed parent, guardian, spouse, adult 25+, or certified instructor. 10) Provisional night restriction — no driving 11 p.m.–5 a.m. for the first 12 months. 11) Passenger restriction — no passengers under 20 for the first 12 months unless accompanied by a licensed driver 25+ (or parent/guardian or instructor). 12) Exceptions — medical necessity, school or school activity, work (with signed notes), or transporting an immediate family member when necessary. 13) Restrictions end — after 12 months (provisional status continues until 18). 14) Why GDL exists — new teen drivers have the highest crash rates; gradual experience reduces crashes. 15) Under-18 phone rule — no use of any wireless device, even hands-free. Score: 14–15 mastery; 12–13 review; below 12 reteach.

weeks.prep: Park the family car somewhere safe and level with the engine off and parking brake set for each in-car session; you hold the keys. Find the owner's manual (or download it). Print a pre-drive checklist (walk-around + cockpit).
misconceptions: Students adjust side mirrors to see the side of their own car. Using the BGE (blindspot/glare elimination) method, push mirrors outward until the car's side just disappears, which shrinks blind spots.
Students ignore dashboard lights that are yellow/amber. Amber means check soon; red means stop safely and address now (e.g., oil pressure, brake, temperature).
Students think mirrors eliminate blind spots. A quick over-the-shoulder head check is still required before lane changes.

days.guide: Sit in the parked car with the student in the driver's seat. Point to and name each control; the student operates it (lights, high beams, wipers and washer, hazards, defroster front and rear, horn, parking brake, gear selector P-R-N-D-L) and explains when it is used.

questions.q: When should you turn on your hazard lights?
questions.a: When your vehicle is stopped or disabled on or near the road, or to warn drivers behind of a sudden hazard ahead; not while driving normally in rain.

questions.q: What gear must the car be in to start it (automatic)?
questions.a: Park (or Neutral), with your foot on the brake.

days.guide: Using the owner's manual, the student identifies 10 dashboard warning lights, their color and the required action, and makes a chart.

questions.q: What should you do if the red oil-pressure light comes on while driving?
questions.a: Pull over safely as soon as possible and turn off the engine; low oil pressure can quickly destroy the engine.

questions.q: What does a solid amber check-engine light mean?
questions.a: A problem has been detected by the engine computer; have it checked soon. A flashing check-engine light means a serious misfire — reduce speed and get service promptly.

days.guide: The student performs the walk-around and cockpit check while you time it, then repeats to improve.

questions.q: Why check behind the car before getting in?
questions.a: Small children, pets or objects may be hidden in the blind area behind the car and could be struck when backing.

questions.q: How should the head restraint be positioned?
questions.a: The center of the restraint about level with the back of the head (ears to top of head), close to the head, to prevent whiplash.

days.guide: Teach BGE mirror adjustment: driver's mirror — lean your head against the left window and set the mirror so the car's side just disappears; passenger mirror — lean to the center and do the same. A family member walks slowly around the car while the student calls out when the person disappears from all mirrors.

questions.q: Where are the car's blind spots?
questions.a: Over each rear shoulder, beside and slightly behind the car (and directly behind the car, low down).

questions.q: How do you check a blind spot?
questions.a: A quick glance over the shoulder in the direction you want to move.

days.guide: The student demonstrates the full pre-drive routine from approaching the car to buckling up, using the checklist. Score it.

questions.q: What are the steps after you are seated, before starting?
questions.a: Lock doors, adjust seat, head restraint and mirrors, fasten seat belt, check passengers are belted, foot on brake.

weeks.assessment_key: Pre-drive checklist key: Walk-around — tires (inflation, damage), lights and lenses clean/intact, no fluid puddles under the car, windows and mirrors clean, nothing behind or around the car (children, pets, objects). Cockpit — doors locked, seat adjusted (feet reach pedals with bent knees, wrists rest on top of wheel, at least 10 inches between breastbone and steering wheel), head restraint level with the middle/top of the head, mirrors adjusted, seat belt on and passengers belted, parking brake on, foot on brake before starting. Proficient = all items performed in order without prompts in under 3 minutes; developing = 1–2 prompts; beginning = 3+ prompts.

weeks.prep: Gather a toy car (or cart), a board for a ramp, a raw egg (in a zip bag to contain mess), a rubber band, and a book as a barrier. Read the handbook sections on seat belts, child restraints and airbags.
misconceptions: Students think a lap belt alone or holding on is enough. Only a properly worn lap-and-shoulder belt (lap belt low on hips, shoulder belt across the chest, never behind the back) spreads crash forces.
Students think airbags replace seat belts. Airbags are supplemental; without a belt a person can be thrown into the deploying bag or out of the vehicle.
Students think short trips are safe without a belt. Most crashes happen close to home at lower speeds.

days.guide: Set the egg 'passenger' in the toy car and roll it down the ramp into a book, first without and then with a rubber band 'belt'. Repeat at a higher ramp. The student explains using Newton's first law (inertia).

questions.q: Why does the unbelted egg fly forward when the car stops?
questions.a: Inertia — the egg keeps moving at the car's speed until something stops it (the 'dashboard', windshield or ground).

questions.q: How does a seat belt reduce injury?
questions.a: It stops the body with the car, spreading force over the strong bones of the hips and chest and lengthening the stopping time.

days.guide: The student reads handbook rules and makes a chart of seat-belt and child-restraint law by age and size.

questions.q: At what age/size can a child ride in a car without a booster seat in California?
questions.a: Age 8, or 4 feet 9 inches tall, if the seat belt fits properly.

questions.q: Who is responsible if a passenger under 16 is not buckled?
questions.a: The driver can be cited.

days.guide: Explain airbag deployment speed (up to about 200 mph). The student measures his or her seated distance from the steering wheel and explains why children under 13 should ride in back.

questions.q: How far should the driver sit from the airbag?
questions.a: At least 10 inches between the breastbone and the center of the steering wheel.

questions.q: Why should a rear-facing infant seat never be placed in front of an active airbag?
questions.a: The deploying airbag strikes the back of the seat near the baby's head with enormous force and can kill the child.

days.guide: The student writes and rehearses a 30-second PSA script with a hook, one statistic, and a clear call to action, then performs it for you.

questions.q: What makes a PSA persuasive to teens?
questions.a: A relatable hook, an accurate, specific fact, and a simple action to take (e.g., 'Click it before you start it').

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test. Grade together.

questions.q: Where should the lap belt sit?
questions.a: Low and snug across the hips/upper thighs, not across the stomach.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (sample): 1) Permit age — 15½. 2) Provisional passenger rule — no passengers under 20 for the first 12 months unless accompanied by a licensed driver 25+, parent/guardian or instructor. 3) Night rule — 11 p.m.–5 a.m. 4) Supervised hours — 50 (10 night). 5) Purpose of the parking brake — hold the car when parked (and as an emergency backup). 6) Red dashboard light meaning — stop safely and address immediately. 7) Mirror method — BGE, outward until the car's side disappears. 8) Children under 2 — rear-facing seat (unless 40 lb or 40 in tall). 9) Children under 8 — car seat or booster in the back seat. 10) Who must wear seat belts — driver and all passengers. 11) Airbag distance — at least 10 inches between breastbone and steering wheel. 12) Explain inertia in a crash — the body keeps moving at the car's speed until something stops it; the belt stops it safely. Score 1 point each; 11–12 mastery.

weeks.prep: Gather index cards and the handbook sign pages. Plan a ride for Day 4 where the student is a passenger with a phone or notebook.
misconceptions: Students confuse the yield triangle and the warning diamond. Yield is a downward-pointing red-and-white triangle; most warnings are yellow diamonds.
Students think a pennant means a school zone. The yellow pennant (on the left side of the road) means No Passing Zone; the five-sided pentagon is the school zone/crossing sign.

Students mix up colors: red = stop/prohibit; yellow = general warning; fluorescent yellow-green = school, pedestrian and bicycle warnings; orange = construction/work zone; green = guidance/directions; blue = motorist services; brown = recreation.

days.guide: The student makes flashcards for sign shapes and colors with the meaning on the back and drills with you until fast.

questions.q: What shape is a stop sign, and why is that shape unique?
questions.a: An octagon; it is the only eight-sided sign so drivers can recognize it from behind or when covered with snow.

questions.q: What does a round yellow sign with an X and 'RR' mean?
questions.a: Railroad crossing ahead.

days.guide: The student sorts 20 regulatory sign images into 'must do' (e.g., stop, yield, speed limit, keep right) and 'must not do' (no U-turn, do not enter, no left turn).

questions.q: What should you do if you see a DO NOT ENTER sign?
questions.a: Do not enter that road or ramp; it is for traffic moving the other way.

questions.q: What does a red circle with a diagonal slash mean?
questions.a: The pictured action is prohibited.

days.guide: The student studies warning and guide signs and explains 10 of them to a family member.

questions.q: What does a fluorescent yellow-green sign with a walking person mean?
questions.a: Pedestrian crossing ahead; watch for people.

questions.q: What do blue signs indicate?
questions.a: Motorist services such as gas, food, lodging or hospitals.

days.guide: On a car ride as a passenger, the student lists or photographs 15 different signs and writes what the driver must do at each.

questions.q: You see a yellow sign with a curving arrow and '25 MPH' under it. What should you do?
questions.a: Slow to the advised 25 mph (or less) before entering the curve.

days.guide: Give the 40-sign quiz. Goal 90%. Review missed signs.

questions.q: What does an orange diamond sign indicate?
questions.a: A construction or work zone warning.

weeks.assessment_key: Sign quiz key: grade 40 signs; 36+ correct (90%) = mastery. Must-know items: octagon — stop; downward triangle — yield; pentagon — school zone/school crossing; round yellow with X and RR — railroad crossing ahead; crossbuck (white X) — railroad crossing (yield to trains); pennant — no passing zone; diamond — warning; rectangle white — regulatory (speed limit, one way); red circle with slash — prohibited action; orange diamond — construction; green — guide/destination; blue — services; brown — recreational areas; DO NOT ENTER — red circle with white bar; WRONG WAY — red rectangle.

weeks.prep: Have the handbook sections on signals and pavement markings, and an online map with street view. Pick three local intersections for Day 4.
misconceptions: Students think a flashing yellow arrow means the left turn is protected. It means turns are permitted but you must yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians.
Students think solid yellow lines are never crossed. You may cross a double yellow line to turn left into or out of a driveway or private road (and to make a legal U-turn), but not to pass.
Students forget what to do when a signal is dark. Treat it as an all-way stop.

days.guide: The student studies each signal type and writes the required action. Quiz orally with quick scenarios.

questions.q: You approach a flashing red light. What do you do?
questions.a: Come to a complete stop, then go when it is safe, as at a stop sign.

questions.q: The traffic signals at an intersection are not working. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat it as an all-way stop.

days.guide: The student diagrams yellow vs. white lines, broken vs. solid, double solid, and the two-way center left-turn lane, labeling what each allows.

questions.q: Can you pass a car across a solid yellow line on your side?
questions.a: No — a solid yellow line on your side means no passing.

questions.q: What do white lines separate?
questions.a: Lanes of traffic moving in the same direction.

days.guide: The student makes a curb color chart with meanings and one example of each.

questions.q: What does a white curb mean?
questions.a: Stop only long enough to pick up or drop off passengers or mail.

questions.q: Can you park at a green curb?
questions.a: Yes, for the limited time posted or painted on the curb.

days.guide: Using street view, the student identifies markings at three local intersections (crosswalks, stop lines, turn arrows, bike lanes) and explains what a driver must do.

questions.q: Where must you stop at a red light if there is a limit line?
questions.a: Before the limit line (white stop line); if none, before the crosswalk; if none, before entering the intersection.

days.guide: Give the signals and markings quiz. Review misses.

questions.q: What does a yellow curb mean?
questions.a: Loading zone: stop only as long as allowed to load or unload passengers or freight; noncommercial drivers usually must stay with the vehicle.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Solid red — stop; right turn after stopping is allowed unless a sign prohibits it. 2) Flashing red — stop, then proceed when safe (like a stop sign). 3) Flashing yellow — proceed with caution. 4) Solid yellow — the signal is about to turn red; stop if you can do so safely. 5) Green arrow — protected turn; still yield to vehicles/pedestrians in the intersection. 6) Signal out — all-way stop. 7) Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions; white lines separate lanes in the same direction. 8) Broken line — passing/lane changes allowed when safe. 9) Double solid yellow — no passing. 10) Two sets of double yellow lines two or more feet apart — a barrier; do not cross. 11) Two-way left-turn lane — center lane with solid outer and broken inner yellow lines. 12) Curbs: red no stopping/standing/parking; yellow commercial loading; white passenger/mail loading; green limited-time parking; blue disabled parking only.

weeks.prep: Draw intersections on large paper (four-way stop, uncontrolled, T, roundabout) and gather toy cars. Read the handbook right-of-way section.
misconceptions: Students think right-of-way is something you take. The law says who must yield; no one has an absolute right, and drivers must yield whenever needed to avoid a collision.
Students think at a four-way stop the larger road goes first. The first vehicle to stop goes first; if two arrive together, the vehicle on the right goes first.
Students think pedestrians only have right-of-way in marked crosswalks. Pedestrians have the right-of-way in marked and unmarked crosswalks at intersections.

days.guide: Using toy cars, model four-way stops, uncontrolled intersections and T-intersections. The student explains who goes first in each arrangement.

questions.q: Car A and Car B stop at a four-way stop at the same time. Car B is on Car A's right. Who goes first?
questions.a: Car B — when two vehicles arrive at the same time, the driver on the left yields to the vehicle on the right.

questions.q: At a T-intersection with no signs, who has the right-of-way?
questions.a: Vehicles on the through road.

days.guide: The student diagrams entering and exiting a roundabout: slow down, yield to traffic in the circle and to pedestrians, enter when there is a gap, travel counterclockwise, signal right before exiting.

questions.q: Which direction do you travel in a roundabout?
questions.a: Counterclockwise (to the right).

questions.q: Who do you yield to when entering?
questions.a: Traffic already in the roundabout and pedestrians in crosswalks.

days.guide: The student reads pedestrian rules and lists where pedestrians have the right-of-way.

questions.q: Does a pedestrian have the right-of-way at a corner with no painted crosswalk?
questions.a: Yes — every intersection corner has an unmarked crosswalk.

questions.q: What should you do when you see a pedestrian with a white cane?
questions.a: Stop and let the person cross; do not honk or call out directions, which can confuse them.

days.guide: The student learns responses to emergency vehicles and school buses, then explains them in his or her own words.

questions.q: An ambulance with siren and lights approaches from behind. What do you do?
questions.a: Drive to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes (if in an intersection, continue through first, then pull over).

questions.q: A school bus ahead has flashing red lights. What do you do?
questions.a: Stop and remain stopped as long as the red lights flash (unless it is on the other side of a divided highway or multilane highway with two or more lanes in each direction).

days.guide: Give 15 written right-of-way scenarios with diagrams; the student answers and explains each.

questions.q: You are turning left on a green light and an oncoming car is approaching. Who yields?
questions.a: You do — left-turning drivers yield to oncoming traffic close enough to be a hazard.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key (examples; full credit requires the correct answer and a reason): 1) Two cars arrive at a four-way stop at the same time — the car on the right goes first. 2) Uncontrolled intersection, cars arrive together — yield to the car on the right. 3) T-intersection without signs — vehicles on the through road have the right-of-way. 4) Turning left at a green light — yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. 5) Entering a roundabout — yield to traffic already in the circle; travel counterclockwise. 6) Pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk at a corner — stop and yield. 7) Blind pedestrian with a white cane or guide dog — always yield; do not honk. 8) Emergency vehicle with siren behind you — pull to the right edge and stop until it passes (do not stop in an intersection). 9) School bus with flashing red lights on a two-lane road — stop from either direction until the lights stop flashing. 10) School bus on a divided highway with a median, you are on the opposite side — you do not have to stop. 11) Merging from a driveway — yield to traffic on the road. 12) Entering from an alley — stop and yield to pedestrians and traffic. 13) Car already in the intersection — yield to it. 14) Funeral procession — yield. 15) Left turn at a four-way stop when another car arrived first — let it go first.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook speed-limit section. Gather a stopwatch, calculator and graph paper. For Day 3 use these assumptions: reaction time 1.5 s; 1 mph = 1.467 ft/s; braking distance ≈ mph² ÷ 20 feet on dry pavement (a common approximation). Build the Unit 2 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think driving the posted limit is always legal. The Basic Speed Law says you may never drive faster than is safe for current conditions (weather, traffic, visibility), even below the limit.
Students think doubling speed doubles stopping distance. Braking distance grows with the square of speed: doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.
Students count 3 seconds from when they pass a fixed object regardless of conditions. Increase the gap in rain, at night, behind motorcycles or large trucks, and when being tailgated.

days.guide: Read the Basic Speed Law together. The student lists five conditions that require slower speeds and explains why a driver going 60 in a 65 zone in fog could be ticketed.

questions.q: Can you get a speeding ticket while driving under the posted limit?
questions.a: Yes — under the Basic Speed Law, if your speed is unsafe for conditions (rain, fog, heavy traffic).

questions.q: Name three conditions that require slowing below the limit.
questions.a: Examples: rain or fog, heavy traffic, pedestrians/children nearby, sharp curves, night, construction zones.

days.guide: The student makes a speed-limit chart and quizzes a family member.

questions.q: What is the speed limit within 100 feet of a railroad crossing where you can't see 400 feet down the tracks in both directions?
questions.a: 15 mph.

questions.q: What is the limit in a school zone when children are present?
questions.a: 25 mph (unless otherwise posted; some zones are posted at 15 or 20 mph).

days.guide: Model: reaction distance = speed (ft/s) × 1.5 s; braking ≈ mph² ÷ 20. The student calculates totals at 25, 45 and 65 mph and graphs them.

questions.q: Calculate the total stopping distance at 25 mph.
questions.a: Reaction: 25 × 1.467 × 1.5 ≈ 55 ft; braking: 625 ÷ 20 ≈ 31 ft; total ≈ 86 ft.

questions.q: Calculate it at 65 mph.
questions.a: Reaction ≈ 143 ft; braking: 4225 ÷ 20 ≈ 211 ft; total ≈ 354 ft — more than a football field.

questions.q: What happens to braking distance when speed doubles?
questions.a: It roughly quadruples.

days.guide: As a passenger, the student picks a fixed object; when the car ahead passes it, counts 'one-thousand-one…'; if your car reaches it before 3, the gap is too small. Note situations needing more space.

questions.q: When should you increase following distance beyond 3 seconds?
questions.a: In bad weather, at night, behind motorcycles or large trucks, when being tailgated, on slippery roads, or when towing.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test. Grade together.

questions.q: What is the maximum speed on most California highways?
questions.a: 65 mph, unless signs post 70 mph.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key (sample 15 items): 1) Octagon — stop. 2) Pennant — no passing zone. 3) Pentagon — school zone. 4) Flashing red — stop then proceed. 5) Signal out — all-way stop. 6) Double solid yellow — no passing. 7) Blue curb — disabled parking. 8) Two cars at a four-way stop together — car on the right goes first. 9) Roundabout — yield to traffic in the circle, counterclockwise. 10) School bus with flashing red lights — stop. 11) Basic Speed Law — never faster than safe for conditions. 12) Maximum on most California highways — 65 mph (70 where posted). 13) Two-lane undivided highway and when towing — 55 mph. 14) Residential and school zones (when children present) — 25 mph. 15) Blind intersections, railroad crossings within 100 feet, alleys — 15 mph. Stopping-distance item: at 45 mph, reaction distance ≈ 99 ft + braking ≈ 101 ft = about 200 ft.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on turns, signals and lane changes. Draw street diagrams with bike lanes and one-way streets. Gather toy cars.
misconceptions: Students turn right from the traffic lane next to a bike lane. In California, drivers should merge into the bike lane no more than 200 feet before the turn (after checking for cyclists) and turn from there.
Students signal at the last second. Signal at least 100 feet before turning, and 5 seconds before changing lanes on a freeway.
Students skip the head check. Mirrors leave blind spots; always look over the shoulder before moving.

days.guide: Demonstrate the three hand signals. The student practices hand and turn signals and explains when hand signals are used (bright sun, signal light out).

questions.q: How far ahead should you signal a turn?
questions.a: At least 100 feet before turning.

questions.q: Show the hand signal for slowing or stopping.
questions.a: Left arm extended out the window and bent down at the elbow.

days.guide: The student diagrams right turns (with and without a bike lane) and left turns from two-way and one-way streets, drawing the path with arrows.

questions.q: Into which lane should you turn when making a left turn onto a two-way street?
questions.a: The lane closest to the center line (left-most lane for your direction).

questions.q: When turning right where there's a bike lane, when may you enter it?
questions.a: No more than 200 feet before the turn, after checking for cyclists.

days.guide: The student lists where U-turns are legal and illegal in California.

questions.q: Can you make a U-turn across a double yellow line?
questions.a: Yes, if it is otherwise legal and safe (no sign prohibits it, you can see 200 feet in each direction).

questions.q: Is a U-turn legal in a residential district?
questions.a: Yes, if no vehicles are approaching within 200 feet, or at an intersection controlled by a sign or signal that protects you.

days.guide: Teach signal–mirror–over-the-shoulder–go. As a passenger, the student practices the head check timing.

questions.q: Why is the head check necessary if mirrors are adjusted well?
questions.a: A vehicle, motorcycle or cyclist can still be in the blind spot, unseen in mirrors.

days.guide: Give the diagram quiz. Review.

questions.q: You are turning left from a one-way street onto another one-way street. Which lane do you start and end in?
questions.a: Start in the far-left lane and turn into the far-left lane.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram quiz key: 1) Right turn with bike lane — signal, check mirror and over shoulder for bikes, merge into the bike lane within 200 feet of the corner, turn into the nearest right lane. 2) Left turn from a two-way street onto a two-way street — start from the left-most lane closest to the center line, turn into the left lane of the new street. 3) Left from a one-way onto a one-way — start in the far-left lane, end in the far-left lane. 4) Right turn on red — complete stop, yield, then turn unless prohibited. 5) Hand signals — left: arm straight out; right: arm out and bent up (or right arm straight out the passenger side not used); slow/stop: arm out and bent down. 6) Signal distance — 100 feet before the turn. 7) Freeway lane change — signal 5 seconds before. 8) U-turn is illegal — on a one-way street, where a 'No U-turn' sign is posted, at or on a railroad crossing, across a divided highway's dividing section, in front of a fire station, in a business district except at intersections or openings, and where you cannot see 200 feet in each direction. 9) Lane change sequence — signal, mirrors, head check, move smoothly if clear.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on lane use, passing, being passed and center left-turn lanes. Prepare scenario cards.
misconceptions: Students think passing is legal whenever the line is broken. Even with a broken line, passing is illegal when approaching hills or curves where you can't see, intersections, railroad crossings, or when you cannot return to your lane safely before oncoming traffic.
Students speed up when someone passes them. Maintain or reduce speed and stay right so the passer can return safely.
Students drive long distances in the center left-turn lane. Enter it no more than 200 feet before your turn, and never use it for passing.

days.guide: The student studies lane choice and explains which lane to use for through traffic, passing and turning on multilane roads.

questions.q: On a three-lane road in your direction, which lane is for faster traffic and passing?
questions.a: The left lane.

questions.q: Which lane should you use if you plan to turn right soon?
questions.a: The right lane.

days.guide: The student lists when passing is illegal and writes the safe passing steps.

questions.q: Name three places you may not pass.
questions.a: Hills or curves where you can't see far enough, within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, across a solid line on your side, where a no-passing sign is posted.

questions.q: How do you know it's safe to return to your lane after passing?
questions.a: When you can see the front of the passed vehicle (both headlights) in your rearview mirror.

days.guide: Discuss what to do when being passed and when a slow vehicle law applies.

questions.q: What should you do when another driver passes you?
questions.a: Stay in your lane to the right and maintain or slightly reduce speed so they can return safely.

questions.q: When must a slow driver on a two-lane road pull over?
questions.a: When five or more vehicles are lined up behind, at the nearest safe turnout.

days.guide: The student diagrams correct and incorrect uses of a two-way center left-turn lane.

questions.q: How far may you drive in a center left-turn lane before turning?
questions.a: No more than 200 feet.

questions.q: May you use the center lane to pass?
questions.a: No.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz. Review.

questions.q: Can you pass on the shoulder to get around a car turning left?
questions.a: No — you may pass on the right only if there's room in a lane without driving off the paved roadway.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: 1) Through traffic on a multilane road — use the right or middle lane; left lane for passing. 2) Passing on the right — only on multilane roads or when the driver ahead is turning left and there's room without leaving the pavement; never on the shoulder. 3) Passing near the crest of a hill — illegal/unsafe. 4) Steps to pass — check that the zone is legal and clear, signal, check mirror and blind spot, accelerate, pass, signal right, return when you can see the passed car's headlights in your rearview mirror. 5) Being passed — stay right, maintain or slow speed. 6) Center left-turn lane — enter within 200 feet of the turn; may also be used to turn left out of a driveway and wait to merge. 7) Slow vehicle with 5+ cars behind on a two-lane road — must pull over at a turnout. 8) Passing a bicycle — at least 3 feet.

weeks.prep: Gather a toy car, a book ramp and a 'curb' (another book). Read the handbook parking section. Find a parallel-parking demonstration video.
misconceptions: Students forget the curb direction for hill parking. Uphill with a curb: turn wheels away from the curb (left). Downhill: turn wheels toward the curb (right). No curb (up or down): turn wheels toward the shoulder (right) so the car would roll away from traffic.
Students think it's fine to briefly park in a disabled space. It is illegal without a placard/plate, with large fines; also never park in the crosshatched access aisle.
Students park too close to hydrants. The minimum is 15 feet.

days.guide: The student lists places where parking is prohibited from the handbook and explains the reason for three.

questions.q: How close may you park to a fire hydrant?
questions.a: No closer than 15 feet.

questions.q: Why not park in a bike lane?
questions.a: It forces cyclists into traffic and is illegal.

days.guide: Use the book ramp and toy car to model the four hill situations. The student turns the 'wheels' correctly and explains each.

questions.q: Parking uphill next to a curb: which way do you turn your wheels?
questions.a: Away from the curb (to the left), then let the car roll back so the rear of the front tire rests against the curb.

questions.q: Parking downhill with a curb?
questions.a: Toward the curb (to the right).

days.guide: Watch a parallel-parking demonstration and the student writes the step-by-step procedure.

questions.q: How close to the curb must your car be when parallel parked?
questions.a: Within 18 inches.

questions.q: What do you do before backing into the space?
questions.a: Signal, check mirrors and over your shoulder for traffic, cyclists and pedestrians.

days.guide: The student learns disabled-parking rules and penalties.

questions.q: Can you park in the blue-striped crosshatched area next to a disabled space?
questions.a: No — it is an access aisle for wheelchairs and lifts; parking there is illegal.

days.guide: Give the parking quiz. Review.

questions.q: You park on a hill with no curb. Which way do you turn the wheels?
questions.a: Toward the side of the road (right), so the car rolls away from traffic if the brakes fail.

weeks.assessment_key: Parking quiz key: 1) Distance from a fire hydrant — 15 feet. 2) Never park — in an intersection, crosswalk, on a sidewalk, in a bike lane, within 3 feet of a sidewalk ramp, in a tunnel or on a bridge (unless permitted), in front of a driveway, on a freeway (except emergencies), double-parked, in a disabled space or crosshatched area without a placard, within 15 feet of a fire station driveway, next to a red curb. 3) Uphill with curb — wheels away from curb (turned left), roll back gently to touch the curb. 4) Downhill with curb — wheels toward curb (right). 5) No curb — wheels toward the shoulder (right). 6) Always set the parking brake and leave in Park. 7) Parallel parking — signal, stop alongside the front car about 2 feet away with rear bumpers aligned, back slowly turning the wheel sharply right until at ~45°, straighten then turn left to swing in, end within 18 inches of the curb. 8) Disabled parking fine — at least $250 and can be much higher (check local amounts). 9) Exit a parallel space — signal, check mirrors and over the shoulder, merge when safe.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on freeway driving and carpool lanes. Print a local freeway map with an interchange. Prepare freeway diagrams for the quiz.
misconceptions: Students slow down or stop at the end of an on-ramp. Use the acceleration lane to reach freeway speed and merge into a gap; stopping is dangerous unless traffic forces it.
Students cross double solid lines into or out of HOV lanes. Enter and exit carpool lanes only where broken lines allow.
Students slow down on the freeway before reaching the exit lane. Signal 5 seconds before, move into the deceleration lane, and then slow down.

days.guide: Using a diagram, the student explains the on-ramp, acceleration lane and merge.

questions.q: Why use the full acceleration lane?
questions.a: To match the speed of freeway traffic so you can merge smoothly into a gap.

questions.q: What should you look for before merging?
questions.a: A gap in traffic, by checking mirrors and over the shoulder.

days.guide: Teach lane choice, scanning 15–20 seconds ahead and maintaining 3+ seconds of following distance.

questions.q: Which lane should slower drivers use on the freeway?
questions.a: The right lanes.

questions.q: How far ahead should you scan on a freeway?
questions.a: About 15–20 seconds ahead (well over a quarter mile at freeway speeds).

days.guide: The student explains how to plan an exit and use the deceleration lane.

questions.q: You miss your exit. What should you do?
questions.a: Continue to the next exit and come back; never stop, back up or cut across lanes.

questions.q: When should you start slowing for an exit?
questions.a: After you've moved into the deceleration (exit) lane.

days.guide: The student learns carpool lane rules and markings.

questions.q: What symbol marks an HOV lane?
questions.a: A white diamond painted in the lane and on signs.

questions.q: Can a solo driver use the HOV lane?
questions.a: Only if the vehicle has a valid exemption (if such programs are in effect) or outside posted HOV hours; otherwise no.

days.guide: Give the freeway quiz with diagrams. Review.

questions.q: How many seconds should you signal before changing lanes on a freeway?
questions.a: At least 5 seconds.

weeks.assessment_key: Freeway quiz key: 1) Entering — check traffic, signal, use the acceleration lane to match speed, merge into a gap, don't stop unless necessary. 2) Signal at least 5 seconds before freeway lane changes. 3) Following distance — at least 3 seconds. 4) Missed your exit — continue to the next exit; never back up or stop. 5) Exiting — signal ~5 seconds, move into the deceleration lane, then slow; observe the ramp speed. 6) HOV lanes — require the posted minimum number of occupants (usually 2+, sometimes 3+) during posted hours; marked with a white diamond. 7) Do not cross double solid lines (two sets of double yellow/white lines two feet apart or more) into an HOV lane. 8) Look ahead 15+ seconds on freeways. 9) Fast lane is the far-left lane; slower traffic keeps right.

weeks.prep: Read handbook sections on sharing the road with pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles, large trucks, buses and light rail. Have a bicycle available to show its size. Print a truck 'no-zone' diagram. Build the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Students think cyclists must ride on the sidewalk or far right at all times. Cyclists may take the lane when it's too narrow to share, when turning left, or avoiding hazards; drivers must give at least 3 feet when passing.
Students assume a truck driver can see them. If you can't see the truck's mirrors, the driver can't see you.
Students think lane splitting is illegal in California. It is legal; drivers must not block or open doors on motorcyclists, and motorcyclists must do it safely.

days.guide: Discuss vulnerable road users. The student learns the 3-foot passing rule and how to merge into a bike lane before turning right.

questions.q: How much space must you give when passing a cyclist?
questions.a: At least 3 feet; if you can't, slow down and pass only when it is safe.

questions.q: What is 'dooring' and how do you prevent it?
questions.a: Opening a car door into a cyclist's path; check mirrors and look back before opening (the 'Dutch reach' — open with the far hand).

days.guide: The student learns why motorcycles are hard to see and California's lane-splitting rules.

questions.q: Why should you look twice for motorcycles?
questions.a: They are small, can be hidden in blind spots, and their speed and distance are hard to judge.

questions.q: Is lane splitting legal in California?
questions.a: Yes; drivers must not block or interfere with motorcyclists, and riders must do it safely.

days.guide: Show the no-zone diagram. The student marks a truck's blind areas and explains wide turns.

questions.q: Where are a large truck's no-zones?
questions.a: Directly in front, directly behind, along both sides (especially the right) and near the cab.

questions.q: A truck ahead signals a right turn and swings left. What should you do?
questions.a: Stay back and do not pass on the right; the truck needs that space to turn.

days.guide: The student learns light-rail rules and the slow-moving vehicle sign.

questions.q: What does an orange triangle with a red border on a vehicle mean?
questions.a: It is a slow-moving vehicle, traveling 25 mph or less (e.g., farm equipment).

questions.q: May you turn left across light-rail tracks in front of an approaching train?
questions.a: No — never turn in front of an approaching light-rail vehicle; obey light-rail signals.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test. Grade together.

questions.q: If you can't see a truck driver's mirrors, what does that mean?
questions.a: The driver can't see you — you are in a no-zone.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key (sample): 1) Signal distance before a turn — 100 ft. 2) Right turn with bike lane — merge into the bike lane within 200 ft. 3) Lane change steps — signal, mirror, head check, go. 4) Passing illegal — near hills, curves, intersections, solid line. 5) Center left-turn lane — max 200 ft. 6) Hydrant — 15 ft. 7) Uphill with curb — wheels away from curb. 8) Freeway lane change signal — 5 seconds. 9) HOV marking — white diamond. 10) Passing a cyclist — at least 3 feet; slow down if you can't. 11) Truck no-zones — directly behind, directly in front, alongside (especially the right side), and around the cab. 12) Truck making a right turn swings wide left first — never squeeze in on the right. 13) Light rail — never turn in front of an approaching light rail vehicle; obey light-rail signals. 14) Slow-moving vehicle emblem — orange triangle with red border (vehicles going 25 mph or less). 15) Motorcycles — look twice; they are hard to see and judge.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on night driving, rain, fog, skids and California hazards (wildfire smoke, high winds, mountain grades and chain controls). Check Caltrans QuickMap to show road conditions.
misconceptions: Students use high beams in fog. High beams reflect off fog and reduce visibility; use low beams (and fog lights if equipped).
Students brake hard when skidding. Ease off the gas and brake, steer gently where you want to go; with ABS, press firmly and steer, don't pump.
Students think roads are most slippery in heavy rain. The first rain after a dry spell is often worst because oil and dust mix with the water.

days.guide: The student learns headlight rules and high-beam courtesy.

questions.q: When must you use headlights?
questions.a: From 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise, when visibility is under 1,000 feet, and when using wipers continuously.

questions.q: When must you dim your high beams?
questions.a: Within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 300 feet of a vehicle ahead of you.

days.guide: The student learns about first rain, hydroplaning and fog driving.

questions.q: Why is the first rain especially slippery?
questions.a: Oil and grime on the road mix with water, creating a slick film.

questions.q: What should you do if you start hydroplaning?
questions.a: Ease off the gas, hold the wheel straight, and don't brake suddenly until the tires regain contact.

days.guide: The student learns skid recovery and explains ABS braking.

questions.q: Your rear wheels skid to the right. Which way do you steer?
questions.a: Steer in the direction you want the front of the car to go (straight down your lane); ease off the pedals.

questions.q: How do you brake hard with anti-lock brakes?
questions.a: Press firmly and hold; let ABS pulse; keep steering.

days.guide: The student learns California-specific hazards: wildfire smoke, Santa Ana winds, mountain grades and chain controls.

questions.q: On a narrow mountain road, which vehicle has the right-of-way when two cannot pass?
questions.a: The vehicle going uphill; the downhill vehicle backs up to a wider spot.

questions.q: What should you do on a long, steep downgrade?
questions.a: Shift to a lower gear to let the engine slow the car and avoid overheating the brakes.

days.guide: Give the hazard scenario quiz. Review.

questions.q: You're driving in dense smoke and can barely see. What's the safest action?
questions.a: Slow down, use low beams, and if visibility is near zero, pull completely off the road, turn off lights except parking/hazards, and wait.

weeks.assessment_key: Hazard scenario quiz key: 1) Headlights required — 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise; when visibility is less than 1,000 feet; when windshield wipers are on continuously. 2) Dim high beams — within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 300 feet of a vehicle you're following. 3) Fog — slow down, low beams, increase following distance, pull off and stop if visibility is near zero. 4) Hydroplaning — ease off the gas, keep the wheel straight, don't brake hard. 5) Skid — ease off pedals, steer where you want to go. 6) Wildfire smoke — low beams, slow down, recirculate air, avoid closed roads, follow evacuation orders. 7) High wind — slow down, grip the wheel firmly, watch for debris and high-profile vehicles. 8) Mountain driving — use lower gear on long downgrades; uphill traffic has the right-of-way on narrow roads; carry chains when required. 9) Blinded by oncoming high beams — look toward the right edge of your lane.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook on scanning, space cushion and the Move Over law. Find dash-cam hazard clips (search 'hazard perception test clips'; preview for graphic content and choose ones without injuries). Make a hazard perception answer sheet.
misconceptions: Students stare at the car directly ahead. Scan 10–15 seconds ahead in the city (about a block) and check mirrors every 5–8 seconds.

Students think the Move Over law means stop. It means move over a lane if safe, or slow down, when passing stationary emergency or tow vehicles or Caltrans vehicles with flashing lights (the law has been expanded to other stopped vehicles with hazards on — check the current handbook).
Students think work zones only matter when workers are present. Fines can be doubled in posted work zones, and lane shifts or equipment can be hazards anytime.

days.guide: As a passenger, the student scans ahead and calls out hazards aloud (commentary driving): pedestrians, cars backing out, brake lights, signals.

questions.q: How far ahead should you scan in city driving?
questions.a: 10–15 seconds ahead, about one block.

questions.q: How often should you check mirrors?
questions.a: Every 5–8 seconds, and before slowing or changing lanes.

days.guide: Explain the space cushion on all four sides. The student draws a car with its cushion and escape routes.

questions.q: What should you do if someone tailgates you?
questions.a: Increase your following distance ahead, move right if possible, and let them pass; don't brake-check.

questions.q: Why avoid driving in another driver's blind spot?
questions.a: They may change lanes into you without seeing you.

days.guide: Watch dash-cam clips, pausing to have the student predict what could happen next and what to do.

questions.q: A ball rolls into the street ahead. What should you anticipate?
questions.a: A child may chase it; slow down and be ready to stop.

questions.q: A parked car's front wheels turn and the exhaust is visible. What could happen?
questions.a: It may pull out; cover the brake and give space.

days.guide: The student learns the Move Over law and work-zone rules.

questions.q: You approach a stopped tow truck with flashing amber lights on the freeway shoulder. What does the law require?
questions.a: Move over a lane away from it if safe; if not, slow down.

questions.q: What is the penalty structure in posted work zones?
questions.a: Fines can be doubled.

days.guide: Give the hazard perception test using 10 clips. Review missed hazards.

questions.q: What's an escape route?
questions.a: An open space you can steer into to avoid a collision, such as an open lane or shoulder.

weeks.assessment_key: Hazard perception test: show 10 clips; score 1 point per hazard identified before it develops plus 1 point for a correct response (e.g., cover the brake, change lanes, increase space). 16–20 = proficient; 11–15 = developing; below 11 = more practice. Key concepts: scan 10–15 seconds ahead; keep a space cushion ahead (3+ sec), behind, and to the sides; identify escape routes; Move Over law; double fines in work zones; reduce speed in work zones.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on alcohol, drugs and driving. Find an impairment-goggles video (e.g., a DUI simulation by a police or safety organization). Parental note: some videos include crash footage; preview first.
misconceptions: Students think coffee, cold showers or food sober you up. Only time lowers BAC (roughly one standard drink per hour).
Students think cannabis makes people drive more carefully. Cannabis impairs reaction time, coordination and lane control, and driving under its influence is a DUI.

Students think a 'little' alcohol is legal for teens. Drivers under 21 may not drive with a BAC of 0.01% or higher (zero tolerance), and it's illegal for them to have alcohol in the car unless with a parent for a legitimate reason.

days.guide: The student researches effects of alcohol, cannabis and certain medications on judgment, vision, coordination and reaction time, and makes a comparison chart.

questions.q: What does alcohol affect first: judgment or coordination?
questions.a: Judgment — impairment of decision-making begins before the person feels or looks drunk.

questions.q: Can an over-the-counter allergy medicine impair driving?
questions.a: Yes; many antihistamines cause drowsiness — read warnings like 'may cause drowsiness; use caution operating a vehicle'.

days.guide: The student learns BAC limits and implied consent.

questions.q: What is the legal BAC limit for drivers under 21?
questions.a: 0.01% (zero tolerance).

questions.q: What is implied consent?
questions.a: By driving in California you agree to submit to a chemical test (breath/blood) if lawfully arrested for DUI; refusing brings penalties such as license suspension.

days.guide: The student researches DUI penalties for minors (license suspension, fines, possible jail/juvenile court, insurance increases, DUI programs).

questions.q: What happens to a driver under 21 who is caught with a BAC of 0.01% or more?
questions.a: One-year license suspension (plus possible other penalties).

days.guide: Role-play refusing a ride from an impaired driver and calling a parent. Agree on a family 'no-questions-asked' pickup plan.

questions.q: Your ride home has been drinking. What could you say and do?
questions.a: 'I'm not comfortable — I'm going to call my parent.' Then call a parent, a sober adult, or a rideshare, and don't get in the car.

days.guide: Give the DUI law quiz. Review.

questions.q: How long does it take the body to remove the alcohol in one standard drink, roughly?
questions.a: About one hour; nothing speeds it up.

weeks.assessment_key: DUI law quiz key: 1) Adult BAC limit — 0.08%. 2) Under 21 — 0.01% (zero tolerance); 0.05%+ can be charged as DUI for under 21. 3) Commercial drivers — 0.04%. 4) Implied consent — by driving you agree to a chemical test if lawfully arrested for DUI; refusal brings license suspension. 5) Under 21 with BAC 0.01%+ — license suspended for 1 year. 6) Under 21 refusing a preliminary alcohol screening test — license suspension. 7) Minors carrying alcohol in a vehicle — illegal unless accompanied by a parent/adult for a legitimate reason (container must be full and sealed). 8) Only thing that lowers BAC — time. 9) Prescription and OTC drugs can impair — read labels. 10) DUI applies to alcohol, cannabis and any drug that impairs.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook section on distracted and drowsy driving. Find an online reaction-time test (e.g., humanbenchmark.com). Build the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Students think hands-free calling is safe. Cognitive distraction remains; and drivers under 18 may not use any wireless device, even hands-free, except in emergencies.
Students think they can multitask. The brain switches attention rather than doing both, increasing reaction time.
Students think opening a window or loud music cures drowsiness. The only remedies are sleep or pulling over safely to rest (a short nap).

days.guide: The student learns visual, manual and cognitive distractions and lists two examples of each.

questions.q: Why is texting the most dangerous distraction?
questions.a: It involves all three types: eyes, hands and mind are off driving.

questions.q: Give an example of cognitive distraction.
questions.a: An emotional phone call or daydreaming.

days.guide: The student reads California phone laws and summarizes them.

questions.q: Can a 17-year-old use a hands-free phone while driving?
questions.a: No — drivers under 18 may not use any wireless device, even hands-free, except for emergency calls.

questions.q: How far does a car travel at 55 mph in 5 seconds?

days.guide: The student takes an online reaction-time test 5 times normally, then 5 times while texting a family member; compare averages.

questions.q: What did texting do to your reaction time, and why?
questions.a: It increased it (typically by tenths of a second or more), because attention was split.

days.guide: The student learns signs of drowsy driving and prevention.

questions.q: Name three warning signs of drowsy driving.
questions.a: Frequent yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting from the lane, missing exits or signs, not remembering the last few miles.

questions.q: What's the best prevention?
questions.a: Get enough sleep (teens need 8–10 hours), avoid driving late at night, and pull over to rest when drowsy.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test. Grade together.

questions.q: What should you do if your phone rings while driving?
questions.a: Ignore it; pull over safely first if you must respond.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key (sample): 1) Three distraction types — visual (eyes off road), manual (hands off wheel), cognitive (mind off driving). 2) Texting combines all three. 3) Drivers under 18 — no phone use, even hands-free (emergency calls allowed). 4) Adults — hands-free only; may touch a mounted phone once with one finger to activate a function. 5) At 55 mph, 5 seconds looking at a phone covers about the length of a football field (≈ 400 ft). 6) Signs of drowsiness — yawning, drifting, missing exits, heavy eyelids. 7) Remedy — pull over and rest or switch drivers. 8) Adult BAC — 0.08%. 9) Under-21 BAC — 0.01%. 10) Implied consent — must submit to testing. Score 90%+ mastery.

weeks.prep: Read the handbook sections on collisions, financial responsibility/insurance and the point system. Review your own family's insurance card. Note: California's minimum liability limits increased to 30/60/15 for policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2025.
misconceptions: Students think they should leave if no one seems hurt. You must stop at any collision you are involved in; leaving is hit-and-run.
Students think insurance is optional if they drive carefully. California requires financial responsibility (usually liability insurance) for every vehicle and driver.
Students think a blowout means slam the brakes. Grip the wheel firmly, ease off the gas, keep straight, and brake gently once under control.

days.guide: The student lists the steps after a collision and practices with a role-play.

questions.q: When must you file an SR-1 with the DMV?
questions.a: Within 10 days if anyone was injured or killed or property damage exceeded $1,000 (regardless of fault).

questions.q: What information should drivers exchange?
questions.a: Names, addresses, driver's license numbers, vehicle registration, and insurance information.

days.guide: The student reads about financial responsibility and looks at the family's insurance card.

questions.q: What does liability insurance pay for?
questions.a: Injuries and property damage you cause to others.

questions.q: What are California's minimum liability limits as of 2025?
questions.a: 30/60/15: $30,000 per person injured, $60,000 per accident for injuries, $15,000 property damage.

days.guide: The student learns the point system and provisional penalties.

questions.q: How many points does a typical moving violation (like speeding) carry?
questions.a: One point; a DUI or hit-and-run carries two points.

questions.q: What happens if a provisional driver gets 2 points in 12 months?
questions.a: A 30-day restriction: they may drive only with a licensed parent/guardian or adult 25+.

days.guide: The student learns responses to brake failure, tire blowout and being stalled on railroad tracks.

questions.q: Your car stalls on railroad tracks and a train is coming. What do you do?
questions.a: Get everyone out and away immediately, moving toward the train at an angle away from the tracks; then call 911 or the number on the crossing sign.

questions.q: Your brakes fail. What do you do?
questions.a: Pump the brake pedal, shift to a lower gear, apply the parking brake gradually, and steer to a safe spot; warn others with horn and hazards.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: You hit a parked, empty car. What must you do?
questions.a: Stop, leave a note with your name and address (and explanation), and report it to local police or CHP.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) After a collision — stop, check for injuries, call 911 if anyone is hurt, move vehicles out of traffic if possible, exchange information (name, address, license, registration, insurance), take photos. 2) SR-1 report — to DMV within 10 days if anyone was injured or killed or property damage exceeded $1,000. 3) Hitting an unattended car — leave a note with your name and address and report to police. 4) Minimum liability insurance (2025) — $30,000 injury/death to one person, $60,000 for more than one person, $15,000 property damage. 5) Negligent operator threshold for adults — 4 points in 12 months, 6 in 24, or 8 in 36. 6) Provisional drivers under 18 — 2 points in 12 months: 30-day restriction (must be accompanied by a licensed parent/guardian or adult 25+); 3 points: 6-month suspension and 1-year probation. 7) Brake failure — pump the brakes, downshift, use the parking brake gradually, steer to a safe place. 8) Tire blowout — hold the wheel firmly, ease off the gas, don't brake hard, pull off when slowed. 9) Stalled on railroad tracks — get everyone out immediately, move away at an angle toward the train, call the number on the crossing sign or 911.

weeks.prep: Find official DMV sample knowledge tests (dmv.ca.gov) and at least one other reputable practice test. Have the handbook. Build the semester final from Units 1–4 keys. Find the DMV online application (DL 44 is now completed online).
misconceptions: Students memorize practice-test answers instead of understanding rules. Have them explain why each answer is correct.
Students rush. The DMV test is not timed tightly; read each choice.
Students think they can skip documents. Bring proof of identity, Social Security number, California residency (2 documents), the driver ed completion form, and parent signature.

days.guide: The student takes a full DMV-style practice test, then reviews every missed question with the handbook page.

questions.q: How many questions are on the California knowledge test for applicants under 18, and how many must be correct?
questions.a: 46 questions; at least 38 correct (verify on the current DMV site).

days.guide: The student rereads handbook sections tied to missed questions and makes flashcards.

questions.q: What should you do when a light turns yellow as you approach?
questions.a: Stop if you can do so safely; otherwise proceed cautiously through the intersection.

days.guide: The student takes a second practice test aiming for 90%.

questions.q: What does a white rectangular sign usually indicate?
questions.a: A regulatory rule, such as a speed limit or lane use.

days.guide: Give the semester final in one sitting (closed book).

questions.q: (After the final) Which handbook section needs another look?
questions.a: Answers vary; plan targeted review before the permit test.

days.guide: The student completes a checklist for applying for the permit and schedules (or plans) the DMV appointment.

questions.q: What documents must you bring to apply for your permit?
questions.a: Proof of identity, Social Security number, two proofs of California residency, the driver education form, and a parent/guardian signature, plus the fee.

weeks.assessment_key: Practice test target: 90%+ on two practice tests. The under-18 DMV knowledge test has 46 questions and requires 38 correct (about 83%) — verify on the DMV site. Semester final: cumulative from Units 1–4 keys; 90%+ mastery. Day 5 checklist key: online application (DL 44 equivalent), appointment, identity document (birth certificate or passport), Social Security number, two proofs of California residency (often parent's documents plus a relationship document for minors), driver education certificate (or enrollment), parent/guardian signature, application fee, vision test, thumbprint and photo, knowledge test.

weeks.prep: Install the American Red Cross First Aid app or open its website. Gather the home first aid kit and a car kit (or a bag to build one), plus a printed kit checklist. Parental note: first aid content includes injuries; keep discussion calm and practical.
misconceptions: Students rush to help before checking the scene. The first step is always to check the scene for safety (traffic, fire, wires, violence); an injured rescuer can't help.
Students think they need a parent's permission to call 911. Anyone should call 911 in a true emergency immediately.

Students fear being sued for helping. California's Good Samaritan law protects people who give emergency care in good faith, without compensation, at the scene of an emergency, unless grossly negligent.

days.guide: Teach Check–Call–Care. Walk through three scenes (kitchen fall, roadside crash, a person collapsed in a park) and have the student say what to check for safety first.

questions.q: What's the first thing to do when you arrive at an emergency?
questions.a: Check the scene for safety before approaching.

questions.q: How do you check if an adult is responsive?
questions.a: Tap the shoulder and shout 'Are you OK?'; check for breathing for no more than 10 seconds.

days.guide: Role-play a 911 call: you play the dispatcher. The student gives location, what happened, the person's condition and care given, and stays on the line.

questions.q: What's the most important information to give a 911 dispatcher?
questions.a: Your exact location (address, cross streets or landmarks), then what happened and the person's condition.

questions.q: When should you hang up?
questions.a: Only when the dispatcher tells you to.

days.guide: The student reads a summary of California's Good Samaritan law and the rules of consent.

questions.q: Do you need consent to help an unresponsive adult?
questions.a: No — consent is implied when a person can't respond.

questions.q: What does the Good Samaritan law protect?
questions.a: People who give emergency care in good faith at the scene of an emergency, without expecting payment, from civil liability unless they act with gross negligence or willful misconduct.

days.guide: The student inventories the home kit against a checklist and builds or restocks a car kit, noting expiration dates.

questions.q: Why include gloves in a first aid kit?
questions.a: To protect both rescuer and victim from bloodborne infections.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Review.

questions.q: List the three emergency action steps.
questions.a: Check, Call, Care.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Emergency action steps — Check (scene, then person), Call (911 / have someone call and get an AED), Care (give care until help arrives). 2) Scene hazards — traffic, fire, electrical wires, water, unstable structures, violence, chemicals. 3) Tell the dispatcher — exact location, what happened, number of people, their condition, what help is being given; stay on the line until told to hang up. 4) Consent — ask a responsive adult; implied consent for an unresponsive person; for a child, ask a parent/guardian if present. 5) Good Samaritan — protects good-faith emergency care without pay (not gross negligence). 6) Standard precautions — gloves, wash hands, avoid contact with blood. 7) Basic kit items — gloves, assorted bandages, gauze pads and roller gauze, tape, elastic bandage, triangular bandage, antiseptic wipes, scissors, tweezers, cold pack, emergency blanket, CPR face shield, tourniquet, first aid guide, emergency contacts, personal medications. 8) Check for responsiveness — tap and shout 'Are you OK?'. 9) Check breathing — no more than 10 seconds. 10) When to call 911 — unresponsive, trouble breathing, chest pain, severe bleeding, seizure, signs of stroke, severe burns, suspected poisoning.

weeks.prep: Get a CPR manikin (borrow or buy an inexpensive one) or use a firm cushion on the floor. Queue the American Heart Association Hands-Only CPR video and an AED trainer video. Have the 'Stayin' Alive' song (100–103 bpm) ready. Note: a home course does not certify the student; Week 23 covers certification.
misconceptions: Students compress too gently or too slowly. Adults need compressions at least 2 inches (about 5 cm, but not more than 2.4 inches) deep at 100–120 per minute, allowing full chest recoil.
Students fear hurting the person. Without CPR, a person in cardiac arrest will die; broken ribs are a possible but acceptable risk.
Students think an AED could shock someone who doesn't need it. AEDs analyze the rhythm and only advise a shock when needed; just follow the prompts.

days.guide: Explain the chain of survival; the student draws it and explains why each link matters (for every minute without CPR and defibrillation, survival falls).

questions.q: Why is early CPR so important?
questions.a: It keeps oxygen-rich blood flowing to the brain and heart until a defibrillator and EMS arrive.

questions.q: What's the first link in the out-of-hospital chain?
questions.a: Recognizing cardiac arrest and calling 911 (activating emergency response).

days.guide: Demonstrate hand position and posture; the student does compressions on the manikin/cushion to 'Stayin' Alive' in 30-compression sets, counting aloud.

questions.q: How deep and fast should adult compressions be?
questions.a: At least 2 inches (no more than about 2.4 inches) at 100–120 per minute.

questions.q: Why allow the chest to fully rise between compressions?
questions.a: Full recoil lets the heart refill with blood.

days.guide: Demonstrate head-tilt/chin-lift and rescue breaths with a face shield on the manikin (1 second each, chest visibly rises). Practice 30:2 cycles.

questions.q: How long should each rescue breath last?
questions.a: About 1 second, just enough to make the chest rise.

questions.q: What if you're untrained or unwilling to give breaths?
questions.a: Do hands-only CPR: continuous compressions until help or an AED arrives.

days.guide: Watch the AED trainer video and walk through the steps on paper: turn on, follow prompts, expose and dry chest, place pads, stand clear for analysis, shock if advised, resume CPR immediately.

questions.q: What's the first thing to do when the AED arrives?
questions.a: Turn it on and follow its voice prompts.

questions.q: What should everyone do while the AED analyzes or shocks?
questions.a: Stand clear — no one touches the person.

days.guide: The student demonstrates 2 minutes of CPR from scene check through compressions/breaths; score with the checklist.

questions.q: How many compressions and breaths are in one cycle?
questions.a: 30 compressions and 2 breaths.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills check (2 minutes): Proficient = checks scene, checks responsiveness and breathing (≤10 s), calls/sends someone for 911 and an AED, hand placement on the center of the chest (lower half of sternum), arms straight and shoulders over hands, depth about 2 inches, rate 100–120/min (count about 30 compressions in 15–18 seconds), full recoil, minimal interruptions, 30:2 with breaths if trained (or hands-only). Developing = 1–2 errors corrected with cues. Beginning = 3+ errors. Chain of survival (adult out-of-hospital): recognize cardiac arrest and activate EMS, early high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced resuscitation by EMS, post-cardiac-arrest care, and recovery.

weeks.prep: Gather a doll for infant practice, a manikin or firm pillow, and a sturdy chair. Practice choking techniques only on a pillow or chair, never with real thrusts on a person. Review the 2025 American Heart Association guideline update: for infants, compressions with two thumbs (encircling hands) or the heel of one hand; for choking adults and children, alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts is now recommended (the Red Cross also teaches this).
misconceptions: Students do abdominal thrusts on infants. Infants (under 1 year) get back blows and chest thrusts only.
Students give back blows to a person who can cough forcefully. If they can cough or speak, encourage coughing and stay with them; act only if they can't breathe, cough or speak.
Students compress infants too deeply or too shallowly. Infant compressions are about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third the chest depth.

days.guide: Demonstrate on a pillow strapped to a chair back: back blows, then abdominal thrusts; then self-rescue by thrusting the abdomen against a chair back.

questions.q: How can you tell someone is truly choking?
questions.a: They can't cough, speak or breathe and often clutch the throat.

questions.q: Where do you place your fist for abdominal thrusts?
questions.a: Just above the navel, below the breastbone, thumb side in.

days.guide: Explain child CPR (age 1 to puberty) differences and practice five 30:2 cycles.

questions.q: How deep are compressions for a child?
questions.a: About 2 inches, about one-third the depth of the chest.

questions.q: If you're alone and didn't see a child collapse, when do you call 911?
questions.a: Give about 2 minutes (5 cycles) of CPR first, then call (unless you have a phone to call on speaker immediately).

days.guide: Practice infant CPR on the doll with the two-thumb encircling technique (or two fingers as older materials show), counting aloud.

questions.q: How deep and fast are infant compressions?
questions.a: About 1.5 inches at 100–120 per minute.

questions.q: How do you give breaths to an infant?
questions.a: Cover the infant's mouth and nose with your mouth and give gentle puffs, each about 1 second, until the chest rises.

days.guide: Practice infant choking relief on the doll: 5 back blows, 5 chest thrusts, supporting the head and keeping it lower than the chest.

questions.q: Why not use abdominal thrusts on infants?
questions.a: They can injure an infant's internal organs; back blows and chest thrusts are used instead.

questions.q: What do you do if the infant becomes unresponsive?
questions.a: Call 911 if not done, begin CPR, and look in the mouth for the object before giving breaths (remove only if seen).

days.guide: The student demonstrates adult, child and infant choking relief and child/infant CPR; score with the checklist.

questions.q: What should you do if a choking adult becomes unresponsive?
questions.a: Lower them to the ground, call 911, and begin CPR starting with compressions; check the mouth for the object before breaths.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills checklist key: Adult/child choking — confirm choking (can't cough/speak/breathe; hands at throat), get consent, call 911 or have someone call, give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades and 5 abdominal thrusts (fist just above the navel, quick inward-upward), repeat until object out or person unresponsive (then begin CPR, checking mouth for object before breaths). Self-rescue — thrust abdomen against a chair back. Infant choking — support head and jaw, face-down on forearm with head lower than chest, 5 back blows, turn over, 5 chest thrusts on the center of the chest just below the nipple line, repeat. Child CPR — 30:2 (single rescuer), one or two hands, about 2 inches (one-third chest depth), 100–120/min. Infant CPR — 30:2, two thumbs (encircling) or heel of one hand per 2025 AHA, or two fingers per older training; about 1.5 inches; 100–120/min. Proficient = all steps correct.

weeks.prep: Gather gloves, gauze, a rolled towel (for packing practice), a commercial tourniquet if available (or a triangular bandage and a stick for improvised practice), a rolled magazine, triangular bandage, and an elastic bandage. Queue the Stop the Bleed overview and an epinephrine auto-injector trainer video. Parental note: some materials show injuries.
misconceptions: Students apply a tourniquet loosely or remove it to check. Tighten until bleeding stops, note the time, and leave it on for EMS to remove.
Students put ice, butter or ointment on burns. Cool with cool running water (not ice) for at least 10 minutes (20 for chemical burns), then cover loosely.
Students wait to see if stroke symptoms go away. Call 911 immediately and note the time symptoms started; treatment is time-critical.

days.guide: Teach Stop the Bleed: direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquet. The student practices pressure and packing on a rolled towel and applies a tourniquet to a family member's arm or a pillow (don't tighten painfully on a person).

questions.q: Where do you place a tourniquet?
questions.a: 2–3 inches above the wound (between the wound and the heart), not over a joint.

questions.q: What should you do after applying a tourniquet?
questions.a: Note the time and leave it in place for EMS.

days.guide: The student learns first aid for thermal, chemical and electrical burns and when to call 911.

questions.q: What's the first aid for a minor thermal burn?
questions.a: Cool it under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, then cover loosely with a sterile dressing.

questions.q: Why must you turn off power before helping someone with an electrical injury?
questions.a: So the rescuer isn't electrocuted; the person may still be in contact with the current.

days.guide: The student splints a 'forearm fracture' with a rolled magazine and triangular bandage sling, then practices RICE on an ankle.

questions.q: How do you check that a splint isn't too tight?
questions.a: Check fingers for warmth, color, sensation and movement before and after splinting.

questions.q: What does RICE stand for?
questions.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

days.guide: The student learns BE-FAST for stroke, signs of heart attack, seizure care, diabetic emergencies and anaphylaxis; watch the auto-injector trainer video.

questions.q: What should you do for someone having a seizure?
questions.a: Protect them from injury (move objects, cushion the head), don't restrain them or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, roll them onto their side after, and call 911 if it lasts over 5 minutes or it's their first.

questions.q: A diabetic person is confused and sweaty but can swallow. What could help?
questions.a: Give sugar (juice, regular soda, glucose tablets) for suspected low blood sugar; call 911 if they don't improve or can't swallow.

days.guide: Give the 10-scenario quiz. Review.

questions.q: A friend stung by a bee has trouble breathing and swelling lips. What do you do?
questions.a: Call 911 and help them use their epinephrine auto-injector in the outer thigh; keep monitoring and be ready for CPR.
